Abstract

The corrosion behaviour of 1913 T240 alloy was studied in chloride solutions[ The pol! arization curve of this alloy showed two breakdown potentials[ The \_rst was related to the dissolution of the coarse intermetallic Al CuMg particles[ A severe Mg dealloying of the particles resulted in Cu!rich remnants[ The matrix surrounding the particles was systematically found to be dissolved[ Indeed\ the particles are surrounded by a dispersoid!free zone which is anodic in comparison to both the rest of the matrix and the S phase particles[ The second breakdown potential corresponded to the matrix breakdown potential[ Pits but also inter! granular corrosion developed[ Grain boundaries were preferentially attacked because they are anodic in comparison to the grain body and the previous dissolution of the intergranular precipitates made them fragile[ Þ 0888 Elsevier Science Ltd[ All rights reserved[
Keywords] Al 1913^ Pitting corrosion^ Intergranular corrosion^ Intermetallics
0[ Introduction

Because of its high mechanical performance and its low density\ 1913 T2 alloy is used in the aircraft industry for numerous applications such as fuselage and door skin\ dorsal \_n and trailing edge panels[ Nevertheless\ this alloy can be a}ected by di}erent forms of corrosion like pitting corrosion\ intergranular corrosion\ stress corrosion cracking or exfoliation corrosion[

It is generally accepted that intergranular corrosion is caused by the development along the grain boundary of an adjacent denuded zone during the precipitation of intermetallic second!phase precipitates in the grain boundary ð0Ł[ If the boundary precipitates are anodic toward the matrix and the precipitate free zone\ they pref! erentially dissolve^ in the opposite case\ the adjacent denuded zone is attacked[ Galvele and De Micheli ð1Ł have studied the in\~uence of chloride ions on the intergranular corrosion of Al!Cu alloys and showed that intergranular attack is not due to a di}erence in corrosion potentials between grain boundary and grain bodies\ but to a di}erence in the breakdown potentials of these phases[

Other investigators ð2Ð4Ł have shown that the anodic nature of the grain boundary region can be attributed to a high concentration of solute atoms in these regions as compared to grain interiors[

In this study\ the corrosion behaviour of 1913 T240 alloy was investigated in 0 M NaCl solution[ The purpose of this work was to understand the susceptibility of the alloy towards intergranular corrosion and other localized corrosion from potentio! kinetic polarization curves[ Speci\_c attention was given to coarse Cu!Mg!rich particles whose corrosion behaviour explains changes occurring in the polarization curves[
1[ Experimental method
1[0[ Material

Corrosion investigations were performed on 1913 T240 alloy supplied in the form of a 14 mm thick plate[ Its composition is given in Table 0[ Specimens were prepared by cutting coupons of 09×09 mm<sup>1</sup> from the alloy plates[ The edges of the specimens were covered with varnish\ leaving a rolling plane area of 099 mm<sup>1</sup> uncovered[ Before testing\ the samples were mechanically polished with 3999 grit SiC paper\ and then with 0 mm diamond paste[ They were \_nally rinsed with distilled water[
1[1[ Potentiodynamic test

All measurements were made at room temperature in naturally aerated 0 M NaCl "pH5#[ The tests consisted of potentiokinetic polarization of the samples from the cathodic potential of −899 mV:SCE to the highest potential of −399 mV:SCE[ The potential sweep rate was 499 mV:h[ All potentials quoted are relative to the saturated calomel electrode\ the counter electrode was platinum[

1[2[ Potentiostatic tests
For several tests\ the scanning potential was stopped at a given value\ and the specimens were maintained at this \_nal potential during various times[ The current versus time was recorded[
1[3[ Phase shiftin\` interferometric microscopy ð5Ł

This method\ based on classical interferometry\ was used to study the behaviour of intermetallic particles through 1D and 2D pro\_les[ As accurate repositioning of the samples was possible\ the pro\_les plotted before and after the test were compared This technique was chosen since the lateral resolution was well suited to the dimensions of the intermetallic particles^ on the other hand\ the resolution in depth was very high] 0 nm[ Consequently\ even slight modi\_cations occurring in the shape of the precipitates or in the matrix around them can be measured[
1[4[ Microscopic observations

After polarization\ specimens were \_rstly examined by optical microscopy[ Then\ observations by scanning electron microscopy "SEM# were performed with a JEOL JXA 5399 in order to study the behaviour of the intermetallic particles[ SEM also allowed the observation and the localization of pits or intergranular attack if the potential reached during the corresponding test was su.ciently high to allow pitting corrosion and intergranular corrosion[ Observations by transmission electron microscopy "TEM# were also performed using a JEOL JM 1909\ in order to examine intergranular precipitation and very small particles[
1[5[ Analysis

Finally\ energy dispersed spectrometry "EDS# analysis was performed during SEM observations to study the evolution of the intermetallic particle composition at di}er! ent potentials[ Likewise\ EDS analysis during TEM observations was used to deter! mine the composition of intergranular and other small precipitates[
2[ Experimental results and discussion
2[0[ Microstructure
Susceptibility to intergranular corrosion and to other localized corrosion forms depends on the alloy microstructure

The rolled high!strength 1913 T240 alloy presents a grain size range between 49 mm and 699 mm^ obviously\ the grains are elongated in the rolling direction[ Both optical and SEM observations performed on alloy 1913 T240 show the presence of a uniform distribution of coarse intermetallic particles throughout "Figure 0#[ They are very large\ their size reaching 29 mm[ The EDS analysis of these second phase particles allows two types of precipitates to be distinguished] more or less spherical Al!Cu!Mg! containing particles and very large and irregularly shaped Al!Cu!Mn!Fe!containing particles[ Such intermetallic particles have also been observed by other authors ð6Ð 00Ł[ The \_rst type was assigned ð6\ 7Ł to the Al CuMg chemical combination "S phase#\ whereas the assignment of the second one was di.cult[ Indeed\ EDS analysis revealed to di}erent chemical phases ð6Ł] ${ \mathrm { A l } } _ { 6 } ( \mathrm { C u } , \mathrm { F e } , { \mathrm { M n } } )$ $\mathrm { \bf A l } _ { 7 } \mathrm { F e } _ { 2 } \mathrm { C u }$ \ or $( \mathrm { A l , C u } ) _ { 6 } \mathrm { M n }$

text: 2[1[ Polarization curve in sodium chloride solution and breakdown potential

Figure 6 shows a typical example of a potentiokinetic polarization curve obtained in 0 M NaCl solution for alloy 1913 T240[ The curve shows two breakdown potentials] the more active one $\mathrm { E _ { b l } }$ \ close to −619 mV and the more noble one $\mathrm { E } _ { \mathrm { b } 2 } ,$ close to −519 mV[ Each of these breakdown potentials presents a rapid rise in anodic current density[

text: As previously explained ð4Ł\ the breakdown potential corresponds to the dissolution potential of a metallurgical phase[ The polarization curve of a given alloy containing more than one phase may indicate the breakdown potential of each phase\ if these breakdown potentials are su.ciently di}erent[ Therefore\ the polarization curve of the given alloy consists of a sequence of rapid rises in current density\ each separated by a region of current stabilisation the length of which depends on the di}erence between the breakdown potential values[ In the polarization curve of 1913 T240 alloy Figure 6\ current stabilisation is not very clear[ Indeed\ only 099 mV separate the two breakdown potentials\ $\mathrm { E } _ { \mathrm { b l } }$ and $\mathrm { E } _ { \mathrm { b } 2 } .$

Galvele and De Micheli ð1Ł have shown that two breakdown potentials can be found in the anodic polarization curve of an aged Al!3)Cu alloy in deaerated 0 M NaCl solution[ The lower one corresponds to the dissolution of the Cu!depleted zone along the grain boundary and the higher one corresponds to the dissolution of the grain bodies[
V[ Guillaumin\ G[ Mankowski:Corrosion Science 30 "0888# 310Ð327

In Fig[ 7\ four micrographs show the remnant S phase particles after potentiokinetic polarization to −589 mV "i[e[ 29 mV higher than the \_rst breakdown potential#[ Some particles were severely attacked\ and a resulting sponge!like structure covered by a more homogeneous layer can be observed "Figure 7a and Fig[ 7b#^ other particles fell out or were entirely dissolved "hole in Fig[ 7c#[ Some S phase particles seem to be partially dissolved "Figure 7a#\ others remain largely intact "Figure 7a and Fig[ 7d#[ As clearly shown in Fig[ 7d\ in the vicinity of the particles\ the surrounding matrix was systematically found to be locally dissolved "Figure 7d#[ On the contrary\ the Al! Cu!Mn!Fe!containing particles\ the matrix and the grain boundary remain unat! tacked[

text: To study the behaviour of the coarse intermetallic particles in detail\ phase shifting interferometric microscopy was performed on alloy 1913 T240[ On and after $\mathrm { E _ { b l } }$ \ S phase particles dissolution was so strong that it was not possible to use PSIM[ So\ to characterise the reactivity of coarse intermetallic particles\ the specimen was polarized for 4 mn at −649 mV\ i[e[ 29 mV lower than the \_rst breakdown potential $\mathrm { E _ { b l } } .$ [ Figure 8b and Fig[ 09b show the 2D pro\_les plotted for a Al!Cu!Mn!Fe containing particle and for a Al CuMg particle respectively after 4 mn at −649 mV\ in 0 M NaCl solution[ The 2D pro\_les plotted before polarization are shown in Fig[ 8a and Fig[ 09a[ In Fig 8a\ the Al!Cu!Mn!Fe containing particle appears in relief whereas in Fig[ 09a\ the Al<sub>1</sub>CuMg particle appears as a hollow[ This is due to the di}erences of hardness between the matrix and the coarse intermetallic particles which leads to such particle relief after polishing[ Figure 00 shows the 1D pro\_les of the same S phase particle shown in Fig[ 09[

\* comparison of Fig[ 8a and Fig[ 8b shows no signi\_cant modi\_cation of the Al!Cu!Mn!Fe!containing particle[ Nevertheless\ the particle has a more strongly marked relief[ This indicates that at potentials lower than $\mathrm { E } _ { \mathrm { b l } }$ \ the matrix dissolves slightly over the whole specimen surface whereas the particle seems to remain undamaged

\* comparison of Fig[ 09a and Fig[ 09b corroborates the hypothesis of matrix dissolution over the specimen surface[ Indeed\ the S phase particle seems to in\~ate The slight dissolution of the whole matrix can be due to the fact that when the sample is directly polarized at −649 mV\ the passive \_lm is not yet formed on the sample surface and consequently the matrix is slightly attacked[ The corresponding 1D pro\_le "Figure 00# shows that the dissolution of the matrix surrounding the particle is deeper than the dissolution of the rest of the matrix[ Indeed\ the sur! rounding matrix was dissolved by about 79 nm whereas the rest of the matrix lost only about 39 nm[ The stronger dissolution of the matrix around the particle explains the impression of the particle in\~ating[ But\ in fact\ at potentials lower than $\mathrm { E _ { b l } , }$ the particle remain unchanged[

text: These results show that the dissolution of the matrix surrounding the Al CuMg particles occurs at potential lower than $\mathrm { E } _ { \mathrm { b l } }$ [ They also show that before $\mathrm { E } _ { \mathrm { b l } } , \mathrm { S }$ phase particles are not attacked[ As we showed previously\ S phase particles are only attacked on and after $\mathrm { E } _ { \mathrm { b l } }$ so\ the dissolution of the matrix adjacent to the particles is not a consequence of particle attack[ As no other phase was found to be attacked between $\mathrm { E } _ { \mathrm { b l } }$ and $\mathrm { E } _ { \mathrm { b } 2 } ,$ the \_rst breakdown potential is assumed to be caused by the preferential dissolution of S phase particles\ and the dissolution of $\mathbf { A l } _ { 2 } \mathbf { C u M g }$ phase is consequently responsible for anodic current density rise[
V[ Guillaumin\ G[ Mankowski:Corrosion Science 30 "0888# 310Ð327

To understand the stronger matrix dissolution at the periphery of the S phase particles at potential lower than $\mathrm { E _ { b l } , }$ observations by TEM performed on coarse intermetallic particles will be useful[ It has been found that Al CuMg particles are surrounded by a $\mathrm { \Omega _ { 1 } \ A l _ { 2 0 } M n _ { 3 } C u _ { 2 } }$ dispersoid!free zone[ The dispersoid distribution is very homogeneous in all the rest of the matrix[ As dispersoids contain copper\ their precipitation depletes the entire matrix of copper^ likewise\ as S phase particles are rich in copper\ their precipitation leads to a preferential depletion of copper in the matrix around them[ Actually\ the dispersoids contain 04 wt) copper whereas the S phase precipitates contain 27 wt) copper\ so the depletion of the matrix surrounding the S phase particles is stronger than the depletion of the rest of the matrix[ Indeed\ EDX analysis showed that the dispersoid!free zone contains 09Ð19) less copper than the rest of the matrix[ It can be assumed that the preferential dissolution of the matrix surrounding the coarse intermetallic particles is caused by the existence of a galvanic couple between\ on the one hand the copper depleted dispersoid!free zone and the rest of the matrix and on the other hand the copper depleted dispersoid!free zone and the Al CuMg particles[ In fact\ S phase particles and the rest of the matrix have both cathodic behaviour in comparison to the copper depleted matrix surrounding the particles[ Warner et al[ ð7Ł observed the same phenomenon on a 1913 T3[

From these results and observations\ it can be inferred that the local dissolution of the matrix surrounding the S phase particles\ which occurs at potentials lower than $\mathrm { E _ { b l } } .$ is caused by the existence of the following galvanic couples] copper depleted dispersoid!free zone:the rest of the matrix and copper depleted dispersoid!free zone:S phase particles[ In both cases\ the copper depleted dispersoid!free zone is the more anodic phase[ This con\_rms that preferential dissolution of the matrix surrounding the Al CuMg particles is not related to the particle attack\ it is only caused by the existence of the galvanic couples[ Now\ it seems more than likely that $\mathrm { E } _ { \mathrm { b l } }$ corresponds to the dissolution potential of S phase[

Observation of Al!Cu!Mn!Fe!containing particles by TEM showed that they are also surrounded by a dispersoid!free zone "Figure 3#[ Consequently\ a selective dissolution of the matrix in the vicinity of these particles may also occur[ Actually\ this preferential dissolution requires much more severe conditions "exposure of the specimen to higher potentials#[ Yet\ the particles always remain practically unattacked "Figure 01#[

The dissolution of the matrix surrounding the Al<sub>1</sub>CuMg particles seems more rapid and severe than that of the Al!Cu!Mn!Fe!containing particles[ Actually\ Elboujdaini et al[ ð04\ 05Ł have shown that the presence of Mg!containing particles has a detri! mental e}ect on the surrounding matrix dissolution and increases this phenomenon[ According to these authors\ the presence of Mg accelerates the cathodic reaction and leads to the formation of alkaline di}usion layers localized around the particles[ Consequently\ it appears more natural that the dissolution of the matrix surrounding the S phase particles is stronger than the dissolution of the matrix surrounding the Al!Cu!Mn!Fe!containing particles[

text: Finally\ the local dissolution of the matrix surrounding the S phase particles is caused by the galvanic couples dispersoid!free zone:the rest of the matrix and dis! persoid!free zone:S phase particles^ it can occur at low potential whereas the dis! solution of the $\mathbf { A l } _ { 2 } \mathbf { C u M g }$ particles occurs on and after the \_rst breakdown potential and before the complete dissolution of the particle can lead to the sponge!like structure covered by a more homogeneous layer[

S phase particle behaviour can explain the current density variations observed when a specimen is maintained after the potentiokinetic polarization at a \_nal potential between the \_rst breakdown potential\ −619 mV and −549 mV[ Figure 02 shows a typical polarization curve of a specimen polarized from −899 mV to −549 mV and maintained for 49 mn at −549 mV[ During the \_rst twenty minutes at −549 mV\ the anodic current decreases and then begins to oscillate slightly[ Ten minutes later\ the current clearly \~uctuates between cathodic and anodic values[ The closer to the breakdown potential the scanning potential is stopped\ the sooner the \~uctuations begin[ For example\ if the scanning potential is stopped at −589 mV\ the oscillations will appear after 7 mn[ It has been previously shown that all the particles do not react alike[ Some of them can be severely attacked or entirely dissolved whereas others remain unchanged[ The oscillations are related to the fact that\ at any given moment\ not all the particles are active[ When few of them are active\ the current is anodic[ When these active particles are completely dissolved or have fallen out\ the cor! responding anodic current disappears\ at least decreases\ and hence the total current is cathodic till other particles begin to dissolve[ It can be proposed that the closer the potential is to −619 mV when stopped\ the smaller the number of active particles\ and the sooner oscillations can appear[

text: EDS analysis of the S phase particles after the potentiokinetic polarization to −589 mV shows a depletion of Mg and an enrichment of copper "Figure 03#[ These analyses were performed on both the porous sponge!like structure and the denser layer] there was no di}erence[ This indicates that Mg selectively dissolves from the Al CuMg precipitates leaving Cu!rich remnants[ The layer could be a copper deposit resulting from the dissolution of the precipitate followed by immediate deposition of dissolved copper on the particle[ Various authors ð06Ð08Ł have observed the deposition of copper contained in the electrolyte or dissolved from particles[ Blanc et al[ ð00Ł who worked on 1913 T240 in sulphate media at higher potentials observed a copper deposit on the particle but also around it[ Indeed\ a copper deposit could explain the copper enrichment of the particle\ but a preferential dissolution of Mg could also lead to Cu!rich remnants[ Buchheit et al[ ð6Ł have also observed a copper enrichment of the S phase particles after immersion of a 1913 T2 alloy in a NaCl solution[ They concluded that dealloying of the particle occurred[ To make a choice between these two hypotheses\ the in\~uence of a few parameters was studied[

text: Referring to Blanc et al[ ð00Ł works\ sulphate ions were added to chloride solution in order to examine if copper deposit around the particles could be observed[ In these case\ copper deposit on the particles would become the preferential hypothesis[ But\ this experiment was not successful and did not lead to any modi\_cation] the layer could always be observed on the particles\ but there were no copper deposit around them[

The same potentiokinetic polarization to a potential 29 mV higher than Eb was run in a NaCl solution acidi\_ed to pH 1[ In these more aggressive conditions\ obser! vations by SEM made 2 hours after the experiment paradoxically show only a slight attack of the Al CuMg particles "Figure 04a#[ However\ some of them had fallen out One day after this \_rst observation\ SEM analyses were performed on the sample[ But at that time\ the particles seemed to be di}erent and the layer had partially and sometimes completely fallen o} "Figure 04b#[ In fact\ at that time the S phase particles really looked like the porous sponge!like structure obtained after polarization to −589 mV at pH 5 "Figure 5#[ Besides observations in Fig[ 6 were made the day after polarization[ The EDS analysis of the particles "after polarization at pH 1# shows a stronger dealloying of Mg\ indeed there was no more Mg in the particles\ whereas the Cu content had increased Fig[ 03[ A lot of particles had fallen out[ It can be assumed that when the attack is strong\ the particle is largely dissolved\ the space between the matrix and the particle increases and sometimes the particle falls out[
V[ Guillaumin\ G[ Mankowski:Corrosion Science 30 "0888# 310Ð327

How could a copper deposit have become altered with time and fallen o}< It is most unlikely[ On the contrary\ a layer with di}erent mechanical properties could be deteriorated during a cycle of $1 0 ^ { - 7 }$ mbar "in the SEM vacuum chamber#:0 bar in natural air "during the $\mathrm { n i g h t } ) / 1 0 ^ { - 7 }$ mbar the day after for analysis[ Actually\ this layer\ with a structure which paradoxically appears less porous than the precipitate below\ may result from the super\_cial cold!work caused by mechanical polishing[ It also underwent the same Mg dealloying[
2[3[ Second breakdown potential] pittin\` corrosion and inter\`ranular corrosion

On and after the second breakdown potential $\mathrm { E } _ { \mathrm { b } 2 } \ \mathrm { ( - } 6 2 0 \mathrm { m V ) }$ \ both pitting and intergranular corrosion developed[ Figure 05 presents several SEM observations of a sample after potentiokinetic polarization to −509 mV "i[e[ 09 mV higher than the second breakdown potential#

Grain boundaries were attacked and large pits developed within the grains[ Some grains were strongly attacked and even the small $\mathbf { A l } _ { 2 0 } \mathbf { M } \mathbf { n } _ { 3 } \mathbf { C } \mathbf { u } _ { 2 }$ dispersoids seem to be dissolved "Figure 05b and Fig[ 05d#[ The pits showed crystallographic facets[ Indeed\ a tendency to grow following certain crystal planes can be observed "Figure 05c#[ Muller et al[ ð19Ł previously observed crystallographically shaped pits in the matrix of an $\mathrm { A l } { - } 3 \% \mathrm { C u }$ alloy in 0 M NaCl solutions[

How can the second breakdown potential be related to both pitting and inter! granular corrosion< All the authors ð1\ 03\ 19\ 10Ł who have studied intergranular corrosion mechanisms of 1913 alloys or Al!3)Cu alloys showed that intergranular corrosion was caused by the dissolution of the copper!depleted zone along the grain boundaries[ This copper!depleted zone only contains 9[1) Cu[ However\ Fig[ 1 shows that no precipitate!free zone was observed along the grain boundaries of the 1913 T240 alloy[ Yet\ EDS analysis of the grain boundary show that it only contains 2 wt) Cu "such accurate analysis was possible with the JEOL 1909 apparatus which allows the utilization of $^ \textrm { a 7 }$ nm analysis spot#[ The same copper content was found over a zone of 19 nm wide on both sides of the grain boundary[ Consequently\ the grain boundary presented as light depletion in copper in comparison with the rest of the matrix which contained 3 wt) copper[

It was seen that two types of precipitate can be encountered in the grain boundary] the $\mathbf { A l } _ { 2 } \mathbf { C u M g }$ hardening precipitates Figure 4\ and the bigger $\mathbf { A l } _ { 2 } \mathbf { C u M g }$ needle shaped precipitates Figure 5[ It was also seen that the dissolution of the $\mathbf { A l } _ { 2 } \mathbf { C u M g }$ coarse intermetallic particles starts at $- 7 2 0 \mathrm { m V } _ { \mathrm { : } }$ \ so the dissolution of the Al CuMg grain boundary precipitates whose chemical phase is the same as that of the coarse inter! metallic particles\ probably occurs at a potential close $\mathrm { t o } - 7 2 0 \mathrm { m V }$ [ Yet\ before $\mathrm { E } _ { \mathrm { b } 2 } ,$ the alloy is not susceptible to intergranular corrosion\ so intergranular precipitate dissolution does not immediately lead to intergranular attack[ So\ it can be assumed that $\mathrm { E } _ { \mathrm { b } 2 }$ only corresponds to the matrix breakdown potential since pits can be observed on the sample surface\ but it also allows intergranular corrosion to develop[ After $\mathrm { E } _ { \mathrm { b } 2 } ,$ grain boundaries could be the preferential sites for the attack in so far as\ the previous dissolution of the intergranular precipitates makes the intergranular sites fragile\ and also\ grain boundaries are more anodic in comparison to the rest of the matrix since they only contain 2 wt) Cu[

Urushino et al[ ð03Ł who studied the intergranular stress corrosion cracking of 1913 analysed the behaviour of the intermetallic compound Al CuMg in 0 M NaCl[ They showed that its dissolution starts at −779 mV[ It seems obvious the anodic dissolution of the Al CuMg coarse intermetallic particles\ and that of the Al CuMg grain bound! ary precipitates cannot occur at exactly the same potential since all these phases di}er[ Coarse intermetallic particles can be encountered in the alloy matrix before the heat treatment whereas grain boundary precipitates are formed during the heat treatment[ Their sizes are very di}erent "19 mm for the coarse particle and around 0 mm for the others#\ and their chemical composition might not be exactly the same[ Urushino et al[ ð03Ł found that the anodic dissolution of the intermetallic compound starts at −779 mV[ It has been found in the present study that the anodic dissolution of the $\mathbf { A l } _ { 2 } \mathbf { C u M g }$ coarse intermetallic particles starts at −619 mV[ Consequently\ the anodic dissolution of the Al CuMg grain boundary precipitates might occur between these two potentials\ or around them[ Anyway\ in both cases $( - 8 8 0 \mathrm { m V } \mathrm { o r } - 7 2 0 \mathrm { m V } )$ \ the two potentials are lower than $\mathrm { E } _ { \mathrm { b } 2 } ,$ so the intergranular precipitates are already dis! solved when the potential reaches −519 mV[

This is why pitting and intergranular corrosion develop on and after the same breakdown potential which corresponds to the dissolution of the matrix both in the grains and in the grain boundaries where precipitates have already been dissolved[
3[ Conclusion

The potentiokinetic polarization curve of alloy 1913 T240 presents two breakdown potentials[ The more active one\ occurring around −619 mV\ is caused by the selective dissolution of the S phase particles[ A severe Mg dealloying of the particles results in Cu!rich remnants[ The $\mathbf { A l } _ { 2 } \mathbf { C u M g }$ particles are surrounded by a dispersoid!free zone[ hence the galvanic couples dispersoid!free zone:the rest of the matrix and dispersoid! free zone:S phase particles cause the dissolution of the matrix surrounding the particles[ The more noble one occurring around −519 mV corresponds to the dis! solution of the matrix and the dissolution of the grain boundaries[ Both pitting and intergranular corrosion develop[ This potential seems to correspond to the matrix breakdown potential[ It also allows intergranular corrosion to develop[ Grain bound! aries are susceptible to preferential dissolution because they are more anodic in comparison to the rest of the matrix and the dissolution of the intergranular pre! cipitates "around −619 mV# makes them fragile[
